The tree in question is a Robinia pseudoacacia, commonly called a False acacia, it is a non native tree from Eastern USA. The mature tree has codominant stems from approximately 2m above ground level and is located in the eastern aspect of the garden. We are proposing to remove this tree completely and therefore remove any risk this tree currently possesses. The tree show some significant signs of dieback in the crown, but more concerningly it has heavy visible decay in the centre of the trunk. A hammer/acoustic test showed a significant column of decay from ground level to approximately 5m above ground level. The decay is likely to extend to a height greater than 5m and throughout the heartwood. The main concern is that this tree is likely to be unstable and could fall causing risk of injury and significant damage to the surrounding structures and trees. The garden is currently undergoing improvements that will include significant additional planting whilst retaining all other architectural mature trees. A native yew hedge has already been planted that offers increased nesting habitat for birds, along with other wildlife benefits. The work will be carried out by a fully qualified, licensed company (Hi-Line) in an appropriate manner.

See images. The English Yew trees have become an issue. Their appearance of being planted closely together indicates they may have originally been intended as a hedge. The trees have been maintained regularly but the cutting back of them has been subject to restrictions, so they have grown very tall and wide over time. This application is to obtain permission to return them back to a hedge height and width. The issues are as follows: - they are situated very close to and overhang an electrical sub-station - phones lines are threaded through them, so this and the above point may cause risks to infrastructure - the amount of material falling from the trees blocks the property's gutters and drains on a regular basis - the debris from the trees covers the public side road, property driveway and path to the front door which, when wet, can be slippery and of concern for the safety of the occupants, especially an elderly resident, plus occupants of next door and visitors to both properties. We are proposing the Yew Trees are cut to a height of 4m and 2 metres wide. This allows for clearance under the phone cables and room for growth, remove the overhang from the electrical substation, and 50cm on the road side to align with the road edge.

proposal: Section 211 notice: proposed works to trees in a conservation area Please accept this as notice under section 211 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 of the following proposed works to two trees at the above address. T1 and T2 are identified on the attached site plan. T1 - mature lime Proposed work: Dismantle to ground level. Ganoderma fruiting bodies have been observed around all sides of the base. On sounding, the lower stem produced a hollow response up to approximately 2.5 metres above ground level. The tree stands adjacent to a frequently used driveway that is also used by third parties. These observations and the exposure of driveway users are the reasons for the proposed removal. T2 - mature beech Proposed work: Reduce to standing deadwood as a habitat monolith approximately 8 metres high, removing the crown and lateral branches. Significant fungal fruiting bodies, identified as Meripilus giganteus, have been observed around the base. This beech shares a rooting system with a companion beech that has previously failed. Potential targets include telephone wires, a driveway and a frequently used garden. The highway may also be within the trees fall zone, depending on the direction of failure. The proposed work would remove the crown while retaining standing deadwood for habitat. The condition of the base and root system, and the stability of the proposed 8 metre retained stem, will be assessed before work proceeds. Please acknowledge receipt, confirm whether either tree is already subject to a Tree Preservation Order, and advise whether the council wishes to inspect them. Given the occupied targets and observed defects, we would welcome an early written response if the council does not intend to make a TPO.
